subtopicTitle: Real analysis — rigorous epsilon-delta, metric spaces

cards.front: State the $\epsilon-\delta$ definition for the limit of a function $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$.
cards.back: For every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that if $0 < |x-c| < \delta$, then $|f(x)-L| < \epsilon$.

Given $\epsilon > 0$, we need $|(2x+1)-7| < \epsilon$. This simplifies to $|2x-6| < \epsilon \implies 2|x-3| < \epsilon \implies |x-3| < \epsilon/2$. So, choose $\delta = \epsilon/2$. If $0 < |x-3| < \delta$, then $|2x-6| < 2\delta = \epsilon$, thus $|(2x+1)-7| < \epsilon$.

cards.front: Define a metric space $(X, d)$, listing the four properties of the metric $d$.
cards.back:
A metric space is a set $X$ with a function $d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ (a metric) satisfying for all $x, y, z \in X$:
1. $d(x, y) \ge 0$ (Non-negativity)
2. $d(x, y) = 0 \iff x = y$ (Identity of indiscernibles)
3. $d(x, y) = d(y, x)$ (Symmetry)
4. $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)$ (Triangle inequality)

cards.front: Define an open ball $B_r(p)$ of radius $r$ centered at $p$ in a metric space $(X, d)$.
cards.back:
An open ball $B_r(p)$ is the set of all points $x \in X$ such that their distance from $p$ is strictly less than $r$:
$$B_r(p) = \{x \in X \mid d(x, p) < r\}$$

cards.front: State the $\epsilon-\delta$ definition of continuity for a function $f: (X, d_X) \to (Y, d_Y)$ at a point $p \in X$.
cards.back:
A function $f$ is continuous at $p \in X$ if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for all $x \in X$, if $d_X(x, p) < \delta$, then $d_Y(f(x), f(p)) < \epsilon$.
This can be rephrased using open balls: for every open ball $B_\epsilon(f(p))$ in $Y$, there exists an open ball $B_\delta(p)$ in $X$ such that $f(B_\delta(p)) \subseteq B_\epsilon(f(p))$.

cards.front: Define a Cauchy sequence in a metric space $(X, d)$ and explain what it means for $(X, d)$ to be complete.
cards.back:
A sequence $\{x_n\}$ in a metric space $(X, d)$ is Cauchy if for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an integer $N$ such that for all $m, n > N$, $d(x_m, x_n) < \epsilon$.
A metric space $(X, d)$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to a point that is also in $X$.

cards.front: What is the key difference in the choice of $\delta$ between point-wise continuity and uniform continuity for a function $f: A \to \mathbb{R}$?
cards.back:
For point-wise continuity at a specific point $c \in A$, the choice of $\delta$ can depend on both $\epsilon$ and the point $c$.
For uniform continuity on the set $A$, the choice of $\delta$ depends only on $\epsilon$, not on any specific point $x \in A$. A single $\delta$ must work for all points in the domain $A$.
